prize_parts.citation: for the optical lattice clock, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength allow frequency standards to be evaluated and compared at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: After the full first round I keep the optical lattice clock as my sole preferred part, and I can now say more precisely why. The idea is one picture: a trapping light whose wavelength is chosen so that it shifts the two clock levels equally, so thousands of atoms can be held still and counted at once without the trap disturbing the very thing being measured. That is a genuine concept, not a refinement of the comb or of ion control. Katori proposed it and realised the first strontium lattice clock; Ye's group at JILA then showed what the many-atom lattice could do, with record stability, systematic uncertainties evaluated at the 10^-18 level and, importantly, the measurement of collective effects such as density and lattice-induced shifts that told the whole field how to build better clocks. Independent laboratories in Japan, the United States, France and Germany compare their clocks with each other, and the agreement at this level is what turns a technique into a test of physics: redshift across millimetres, limits on drifting constants, searches for ultralight dark matter. That cross-checked, reproduced precision is the standard I apply. I do not require the redefinition of the second as a precondition; the physics is already in hand. B014 is a worthy alternative and I would accept it, but I rank it second because its central question, why the superconductivity occurs, is still open.
statement.case_against: The strongest objections are still three. First, overlap: the comb (2005) and ion quantum control (2012) are close neighbours, and a reader may see the lattice clock as the next instrument in a lineage rather than a discovery of something new in nature. I think the citation can be worded narrowly around the magic-wavelength lattice to answer this, but I accept that colleagues who weigh novelty of phenomenon over novelty of concept will not be persuaded. Second, credit: the Paris, PTB, JILA and RIKEN groups made decisive contributions, and I am relying on memory for the order of the first demonstrations, so I cannot exclude that a third name belongs; a request for an outside expert opinion on priority is warranted. Third, my own field is atomic physics, so I may overweight the elegance of the idea and underweight the claims of a field I know less well.

responses.point: Pearce asks whether Ye's contribution is primarily the lattice clock itself or is still shaded by the frequency-comb work, which decides whether the pair is really Katori and Ye, and he also pairs the clock with a one-name IceCube part.
responses.response: My answer is that Ye's credit for the lattice clock stands on its own. The comb was a tool he inherited from the Hall laboratory and it is not what the citation would name. What Ye's group did with the strontium lattice is different in kind: they pushed the clock to record stability and accuracy, characterised the shifts that limit it, and compared it with other clocks. That is lattice-clock physics, not comb physics. I would therefore keep Katori and Ye, with Katori credited for the concept and the first realisation and Ye for taking it to the 10^-18 level. On the two-part proposal, I do not think the clock needs a partner, and I cannot support B016 with a single credited name until experts show that this is a fair attribution for a collaboration with AMANDA behind it. I would suggest the chair not carry B016 unless that is resolved.

responses.point: Eriksson calls the clock precision engineering built on the 2005 comb recognition, whereas twisted bilayer graphene opens a new space of quantum phases.
responses.response: I understand the distinction and I do not dismiss it, but I think it undersells the magic-wavelength idea. The difficulty of a lattice clock was that trapping light normally shifts the levels and ruins accuracy; seeing that a particular wavelength cancels this to first order is a physical insight, not engineering. It also turned out that the many-atom lattice carries its own physics, with interactions and collective shifts that had to be understood. I agree with him on one point: a citation that sounded like a general prize for better clocks would deserve his objection, which is why I want the wording tied to the lattice and the magic wavelength. On twisted graphene I accept his argument that a reproduced phenomenon need not wait for its mechanism. That moves B014 closer to my first choice than it was in round 1, but my worry about disorder and the open pairing mechanism has not yet been answered by anything I have read.

responses.point: Mehlig separates the discovery from the explanation: the citation would name the prediction of flat bands and the observed correlated and superconducting phases, not a pairing mechanism, and the flat-band mechanism is the well-understood part.
responses.response: This is the most useful reply to my round-1 concern and I partly accept it. If the citation names only the prediction and the observed phases, my maturity objection is much weaker, because the continuum model is transparent and the phases are seen by several groups and probes. What would move me further is evidence from the condensed matter members that the correlated insulating and superconducting states are reproducible in their essentials across samples, so that twist-angle disorder affects details rather than the existence of the phases. I also note the chair's question about Andrei: if outside experts judge that her STM flat-band evidence was an independent discovery and not corroboration, the trio is not clean, and I would then be reluctant to prefer B014. I still read the clock as having the clearer allocation of credit, but I would no longer oppose B014 as a prize.

responses.point: Kroll, who shares my preferred part, describes the lattice clock as a measurement advance with a clean Katori and Ye pairing, and raises the SI redefinition and Ye's Hall lineage as the open points.
responses.response: We agree on the pair and the systematics. On the question of whether the clock is a discovery or a capability, I would say the committee has precedent for rewarding a new way of measuring when it opens physics that could not be seen before, and the lattice clock does this through its redshift, constant and dark-matter tests, although I concede that the most striking new-physics result has not yet arrived. We disagree slightly on the redefinition of the second: I would not make it a condition, since waiting for a metrological body is not a scientific criterion. If the committee does want a demonstrated new-physics result as a condition, then I would accept that B014 is the stronger candidate and would not fight for the clock.

responses.point: Danielsson has moved from IceCube to B014 but keeps B016 as his first alternative, and he is concerned about the maturity of twisted bilayer graphene's interpretation.
responses.response: I defer to him on neutrino astronomy and I share his view that observing something new in nature is what the prize does best. His move to B014 shows that the leading position rests on scientific reasoning. I agree with him that the pairing mechanism is a real risk, which is the reason I stay with the clock for now. On B016 my position is unchanged: the discovery is real, but a single name for a km3 collaboration with AMANDA predecessors is hard for me to defend, and I would need him and the chair to name a second credited person that experts can support.

uncertainties: Who beyond Katori and Ye, if anyone, belongs to the lattice-clock credit (Lemonde, Lisdat, Sterr, Ludlow and the Paris, PTB and JILA groups); I am relying on memory for the priority of the first strontium demonstrations and an outside expert report is needed.

Whether the committee reads the lattice clock as a discovery or as a measurement capability, and whether the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is disqualifying for a citation worded narrowly around the lattice.
Whether Andrei's early STM work on flat bands in twisted graphene was an independent discovery or corroboration, and whether Cao's first authorship should change the credited set for B014.
How reproducible the correlated and superconducting phases of twisted bilayer graphene are across samples, given twist-angle disorder; this decides whether I would move B014 to first place.
Whether a defensible second credited name exists for B016, which I cannot judge as a non-expert.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I am a long-time collaborator of Anne L'Huillier, the 2023 laureate, and have co-authored with the Lund group and Ursula Keller's group, but none of them is a credited name in my configuration or in any shortlisted part. I have no collaboration with Katori or Ye. Atomic physics is my home field and is close to B013, B031 and B017, which I flag as a possible bias in favour of B013 and not as a recusal; I have asked colleagues to weigh my preference with that in mind.
